name: Pharmacogenomics
title: Pharmacogenomics
answer: Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation affects drug response, including efficacy, dosing, and adverse reactions. In the context of artificial intelligence, it covers models that predict phenotype from genotype, annotate variants, and support prescribing decisions. The field sits within genomic medicine and precision therapeutics, bridging clinical pharmacology and molecular diagnostics. It includes germline and somatic variation relevant to drug metabolism, transport, and target pathways. Professionals use these systems to interpret test results and flag actionable gene-drug pairs.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation affects drug response, including efficacy, dosing, and adverse reactions. In the context of artificial intelligence, it covers models that predict phenotype from genotype, annotate variants, and support prescribing decisions. The field sits within genomic medicine and precision therapeutics, bridging clinical pharmacology and molecular diagnostics. It includes germline and somatic variation relevant to drug metabolism, transport, and target pathways. Professionals use these systems to interpret test results and flag actionable gene-drug pairs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Models typically run on standard clinical computing infrastructure, including electronic health record systems, laboratory information systems, and cloud or on-premises servers. Inputs are structured genetic test results, often in VCF or star-allele notation, plus patient demographics and medication lists. Many implementations rely on curated knowledge bases such as PharmGKB and CPIC guidelines rather than large neural networks. Compute requirements are modest compared to imaging or language models, so deployment can be local to a hospital or reference laboratory.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core work is rule-based or machine learning classification that maps genotypes to predicted metabolizer status, such as poor, intermediate, normal, or ultrarapid. Curators and clinical pharmacologists translate published evidence into decision rules for specific gene-drug pairs. Some newer models use supervised learning on biobank or electronic health record data to discover or refine associations. Validation typically compares predicted phenotype or dose recommendation against measured drug levels, clinical outcomes, or expert consensus.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Pharmacogenomic models carry risk of incorrect phenotype assignment, missed interactions, and over-reliance on incomplete variant panels. Data provenance matters because allele definitions and evidence grades change over time, and a model trained on one population may not transfer to another. Regulatory oversight varies by jurisdiction, with some tests cleared as in vitro diagnostics and others offered as laboratory-developed tests. Patient consent, genetic data privacy, and return of incidental findings are central governance concerns. The site tracks 210 compliance and regulation pages relevant to this area, reflecting active rulemaking and guidance.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving from single-gene rules toward polygenic scores and combined clinical-genetic models that predict drug response across multiple medications. Integration with electronic health records and clinical decision support is likely to become more automated, with preemptive genotyping rather than reactive single-gene testing. Research is also exploring how large language models can summarize pharmacogenomic evidence for clinicians, though clinical use remains cautious. Over time, models may incorporate rare variants, structural variation, and drug-drug-gene interactions to improve dosing in diverse populations.
